reason: Partly creeping: the value is creeping (FLOPO:0991009) with an approximate qualifier, as for 'sub-' words; no separate term is needed.
Semilunate = half-moon shaped, the botanical crescent (lunate already maps to PATO:0001870, RELATED synonym lunate in the previous review).
A loose comparison on a generic 'appendage'; no definite shape, and the bearer itself is not a usable part.
A count inside a word: vascular bundle (PO_0005020) amount 1 on the sepal or leaflet, via the reviewed 'nerved' ending.
Bark sloughing in scales = outer layers shed in flakes, which the definition of exfoliating covers.
A spire-like crown or inflorescence is narrowly cone-shaped, tapering to a point; the tall and narrow part of the meaning is lost.
A 'stag's-horn' process is branched like an antler; branched states the quality without a one-off analogy term.
Two statements at once: the branchlet is finely tomentose (PATO_0002341) and its hairs (trichome PO_0000282) are stellate; no single term should fuse hair type and density.
Exfoliating is defined as outer layers peeling in sheets, strips, plates or flakes, with 'peeling' as a synonym.
The botanical apex shape; not PATO:0002091 subacute, which is a disease time course. The French 'sub-aiguës' is the same word.
Two values run together: filiform (PATO_0104351) and relatively thick; the comparison has no stated reference, so only filiform is safe.
Thorned stems bear thorns: thorn present, like lenticellate and stipulate in the previous review.

States that trichosclereids are present; PO has no sclereid or trichosclereid class, so the nearest part is idioblast (a trichosclereid is an idioblastic sclereid). A PO request for the class would be better.
A blade three times pinnately divided is tripinnate.
'1 triple' is a fragment, and 'triple spines' could mean spines in threes or spines forked into three; too unclear to map.
Flowers or pedicels borne in small umbels from about one point, which the definition of umbelliform covers.
Two surface values together: warty (PATO_0001361, the rule for verrucose) and finely rugose (PATO_0001359); each is annotated, not a fused term.
Wedge-shaped is an EXACT synonym of cuneate; cuneiform has the same rule in the previous review.
Gland maps to portion of secretory tissue (previous rule C265); the absence holds for the anther apex, which should be the bearer.
It denies only black dots at the margin, not dots or glands in general; reducing it to 'gland absent' would be false for petals with pale dots.
PO uses 'cross-vein' as a synonym of four different vein orders, and on glumes it means transverse veins; any choice of PO class would be a guess.
A swelling is not a part with a PO class, and the statement only makes sense in its key context.
Papilla maps to papilla cell (previous rule C269); 'without' states its absence.
Setae was rejected as a generic part (config/flora_rejected_bearer_words.tsv); on a pappus they are pappus bristles, not trichomes.
States that the leaf or leaflet has no stipels; the class exists in PO.
'Appendage' is a generic part with no PO class; its absence cannot be stated without knowing which structure it is.
A relation stated without its second term ('at or near the top of the filament'); the full sentence belongs to docs/odp/09-relation-to-another-part.md.
An outline broadest near the middle is elliptic, as opposed to ovate (broadest below) and obovate (broadest above).
Crispulate = finely crisped; crisped is already defined as finely and irregularly curled.
A shape between elliptic (PATO_0000947) and ovate (FLOPO:0991024), written as one word; like 'oblong-ovate', it is a compound of two values, not a new term.
